evidence.note: Up front, correctly names the task as 'massive' and enumerates the major subsystems (S3 data plane+SigV4, admin API, console, lifecycle worker, notifications, audit, multi-tenancy); the 'Plan:' lines lay out a sensible foundational-first build order: storage helpers -> tenant/auth -> SigV4 -> S3 routes -> admin -> console -> workers.

Instead of sizing verifiable increments, wrote the entire ~3000-line monolith in one continuous append pass before any execution/test. Foundational risk (SigV4) was buried in the dump rather than isolated and validated first, which later forced the long rework loop.

A de-facto dependency-aware verification order emerges reactively: basic CRUD -> multipart/versioning/tagging -> presigned -> admin API -> console API -> bucket configs -> cross-tenant/edge cases -> testids. Each feature has a concrete acceptance check (e.g. step 90 multipart composite ETag, step 110 206/416 ranged reads), but these were rolling per-feature checks, not a pre-declared milestone hierarchy with done-criteria.

Concurrency (30 clients), lifecycle worker, and notification worker were repeatedly flagged as 'still need to verify' but never clearly closed out with an explicit done-check before the two Submit steps — showing the milestone tracking was informal and left foundational requirements unconfirmed.

reasoning: The agent enumerated the dozen subsystems and pursued a broadly sensible foundations-first order (auth/storage before dependents), matching the level-5 anchor, and its per-feature verification often carried a concrete done-check (composite ETag, 206/416), reaching toward the 8 anchor's acceptance-check quality. But it never front-loaded the hardest unknown (SigV4) as an isolated first milestone — it dumped a full monolith before any test, then discovered the signing risk reactively — and there was no explicit, dependency-ordered milestone hierarchy or living plan; concurrency and the workers were left as unverified 'still need to' items at submit. That places it solidly at 5 rather than 8.
